pages.x: For decades Central America was ruled by landowners and generals, often backed by the United States. In Nicaragua one family, the Somozas, had held power since the 1930s and owned much of the country. When an earthquake flattened the capital, Managua, in 1972, Anastasio Somoza was accused of pocketing the aid sent from abroad.

The Sandinistas, guerrillas named after Augusto Sandino, a rebel of the 1920s, led a nationwide rising in 1979. On 17 July Somoza fled to Miami, and two days later the rebels rode into Managua in triumph. They set out to share land, and to teach the whole country to read.

In El Salvador a military government fought a growing rebellion, and death squads murdered priests, unionists and peasants. Archbishop Óscar Romero spoke out on the radio each week, and begged soldiers to stop the killing. On 24 March 1980 he was shot dead as he said Mass. In 2018 the Catholic Church made him a saint.

The rebels had united as the FMLN, and held large parts of the countryside. In December 1981 an army battalion trained by the United States killed almost every man, woman and child in the village of El Mozote. The government denied it for years, until forensic experts dug up the remains.

Guatemala's war had begun in 1960. In the early 1980s, under General Efraín Ríos Montt and his predecessor, the army's campaign against the guerrillas destroyed hundreds of Maya villages in the highlands. A truth commission backed by the UN later found that the state had committed acts of genocide.
pages.of: killed or vanished in Guatemala's war

pages.x: Daniel Ortega, the Sandinista leader, was elected president of Nicaragua in 1984. But the United States under Ronald Reagan saw his government as a Soviet foothold, and armed the Contras, rebels built around Somoza's old National Guard, who raided Nicaragua from Honduras. When Congress cut off their money, officials secretly sold arms to Iran to pay for them.

Costa Rica's president, Óscar Arias, persuaded the region's leaders to sign a peace plan in 1987, and won the Nobel Peace Prize. In 1990 Nicaraguans voted the Sandinistas out, and they handed over power. El Salvador's war ended in 1992, and Guatemala's, the longest, in December 1996.

Most of the dead were civilians, and the truth commissions of El Salvador and Guatemala found that most had been killed by the army and the death squads. Millions fled, many to the United States. Few of those responsible were ever punished, and violence and poverty still drive people from the region.
